title: Causal Imitation Learning under Expert-Observable and Expert-Unobservable Confounding
claim: Hidden confounders split into expert-observable and expert-unobservable parts, and both affect actions and states, which makes naive imitation biased.
layout: Single causal graph, two time slices left-to-right, confounders on top, red dashed edges
description: A single causal DAG of an MDP over two consecutive time steps. Along the bottom are blue state nodes (s_{t-1}, s_t, s_{t+1}) and orange action nodes (a_{t-1}, a_t). Solid black arrows link states to actions through the expert policy π_E, and link states and actions to the next state. Curved solid arrows run directly from each state to the one after next. Green reward nodes (r_{t-1}, r_t) sit above, with solid arrows coming in from the state and action. At the top, each time step has a dashed ellipse labeled u_{t-1} or u_t. Each ellipse holds two dark-gray confounder nodes, u^o and u^ε. Black dashed arrows run from u^o to the reward, the action and the next state. Red dashed arrows run from u^ε to the action and the next state. A dashed arrow links the two ellipses. The eye goes first to the dark top nodes and the red arrows, then to the colored node rows.

abstract: We propose a general framework for causal Imitation Learning (IL) with hidden confounders, which subsumes several existing settings. Our framework accounts for two types of hidden confounders: (a) variables observed by the expert but not by the imitator, and (b) confounding noise hidden from both. By leveraging trajectory histories as instruments, we reformulate causal IL in our framework into a Conditional Moment Restriction (CMR) problem. We propose DML-IL, an algorithm that solves this CMR problem via instrumental variable regression, and upper bound its imitation gap. Empirical evaluation on continuous state-action environments, including Mujoco tasks, demonstrates that DML-IL outperforms existing causal IL baselines.
